item.title: CVE-2026-114149: How a Counter Mismatch Became a $10,000 MSRC Bounty
item.description:
On November 10, 2026, Microsoft published CVE-2026-114149, a denial-of-service vulnerability in ASP.NET Core multipart form processing.

This was the first vulnerability I submitted to MSRC that received a bounty. MSRC assessed it as Important / Denial of Service and awarded $10,000 under the .NET Bounty Program. The public advisory rates it High, with a CVSS 3.1 base score of 7.5, and classifies it as CWE-770: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling.
item.content:
On November 10, 2026, Microsoft published CVE-2026-114149, a denial-of-service vulnerability in ASP.NET Core multipart form processing.

This was the first vulnerability I submitted to MSRC that received a bounty. MSRC assessed it as Important / Denial of Service and awarded $10,000 under the .NET Bounty Program. The public advisory rates it High, with a CVSS 3.1 base score of 7.5, and classifies it as CWE-770: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling.

The bug itself is not complicated. The interesting part is how a seemingly reasonable header-count limit became completely ineffective because the implementation counted the wrong unit.

This post is based on Microsoft’s public advisory and public fix. It includes only a minimal root-cause demonstration and does not provide a concurrency stress tool or a production-targeting exploit.

TL;DR

ASP.NET Core’s MultipartReader limits each multipart section to 16 header lines by default. The vulnerable implementation enforced that limit with KeyValueAccumulator.KeyCount, which counts distinct header names, not the actual number of header lines.

By repeating a single header name, an unauthenticated attacker could make the parser accept far more header lines than configured while retaining every value. In my test:

Metric Observed result
Request size 25,675,697 bytes
Multipart sections 1,024
Duplicate headers per section 5,000
Total retained duplicate values 5,120,000
Cumulative managed allocation 2,431,139,200 bytes
Peak working set 238,432,256 bytes
Cumulative allocation amplification 94.7x
Peak working-set amplification 9.3x

The request required no authentication and remained below Kestrel’s default 30 MB request-body limit.

Background: What the Multipart Limit Is Supposed to Count

When an application processes a file upload or another multipart/form-data request, ASP.NET Core divides the request body into sections. Each section has its own headers, for example:

Content-Disposition: form-data; name="file"; filename="demo.txt"
Content-Type: text/plain

MultipartReader.HeadersCountLimit, configured through FormOptions.MultipartHeadersCountLimit, limits the number of headers allowed in each section. Its default value is 16. The limit is intended to prevent the parser from accepting and retaining an excessive number of header lines in a single section.

The problem was the definition of “count.”

The relevant part of the old MultipartReader.ReadHeadersAsync implementation can be reduced to:

var accumulator = new KeyValueAccumulator();

// For every multipart header line read:
accumulator.Append(name, value);

if (accumulator.KeyCount > HeadersCountLimit)
{
    throw new InvalidDataException(
        $"Multipart headers count limit {HeadersCountLimit} exceeded.");
}

KeyValueAccumulator combines multiple values that use the same key. Given these lines:

A: one
A: two
A: three

the parser reads three header lines and stores three values, but KeyCount remains 1.

The security control was meant to limit header lines, while the implementation checked distinct header names. Those units are not equivalent, and repeated names bypassed the limit.

Minimal Root-Cause Validation

The following example does not create meaningful memory pressure. It only demonstrates the counting error. Before the fix, a section containing three header lines was accepted with the limit set to 2 because it contained only two distinct names: Content-Disposition and A.

using System.Text;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.WebUtilities;

const string boundary = "demo-boundary";
var body =
    $"--{boundary}\r\n" +
    "Content-Disposition: form-data; name=\"file\"; filename=\"x\"\r\n" +
    "A: one\r\n" +
    "A: two\r\n" +
    "\r\n" +
    "\r\n" +
    $"--{boundary}--\r\n";

await using var stream = new MemoryStream(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(body));
var reader = new MultipartReader(boundary, stream)
{
    HeadersCountLimit = 2
};

var section = await reader.ReadNextSectionAsync();
Console.WriteLine(section is not null);

On a vulnerable version, the section is parsed successfully. On a fixed version, the third header line causes an InvalidDataException.

I also used a small differential control to isolate the mechanism:

  • With HeadersCountLimit = 1, A + A was accepted because KeyCount == 1.
  • With the same limit, A + B was rejected on the second line because the distinct-key count became 2.

This control tied the behavior specifically to duplicate names not incrementing KeyCount, rather than to request size, Kestrel configuration, or an environmental artifact.

From a Logic Error to Measurable Security Impact

Showing that a limit uses inconsistent semantics is not enough to establish denial-of-service impact. The next stage had to answer three questions:

  1. Can a remote attacker control the relevant input?
  2. Are the extra header values actually retained and allocated?
  3. Is the additional resource consumption attributable to this defect rather than to ordinary multipart parsing?

Common ASP.NET Core upload paths enter the affected multipart parser when an application reads Request.Form, binds an IFormFile, or otherwise invokes FormFeature. No authentication is inherently required; the attacker only needs access to an endpoint that parses a multipart/form-data request.

The duplicate values are retained in the section’s header collection. For file sections, they are also preserved through FormFile.Headers. A short repeated header line therefore creates allocations for strings, collection growth, and value aggregation that are much larger than its wire representation.

My end-to-end test used 1,024 zero-byte file sections with 5,000 short duplicate headers in each section. One important detail is that MultipartHeadersCountLimit is enforced per section: each section presented 5,000 lines against the default limit of 16. The 5,120,000 figure is the total number of retained duplicate values across all sections, not a claim that values from different sections share one counter.

On ASP.NET Core 10.0.11 under Kestrel, a request of approximately 25.7 MB caused approximately 2.43 GB of cumulative managed allocation and a peak working set of about 238 MB. With correct line counting, parsing stops as soon as a section exceeds 16 header lines, preventing the later amplification.

Why the Report Qualified for a Bounty

Resource consumption is not automatically a security vulnerability. For this class of report, the difficult part is usually not producing a large number; it is proving that the security impact is attributable to a specific defect.

This report had several important properties:

  • A named limit was completely bypassed: a configured limit of 16 still allowed thousands of same-name header lines.
  • The default configuration was reachable: exploitation did not require disabling request limits or enabling unusual options.
  • The path was remote and unauthenticated: a normal multipart form-processing endpoint was sufficient.
  • The minimal control was discriminating: A + A and A + B differed only in whether the header name was repeated.
  • The impact was quantified: the report separately recorded request size, cumulative allocation, peak working set, retained-value count, and elapsed time.
  • The remediation removed the impact: changing the counter from distinct keys to total appended values stopped the request at the configured boundary.

The main lesson is not to submit only “this code looks wrong” or “memory usage increased.” A report that is easy to validate needs a connected evidence chain from root cause and controlled input to the affected resource, observable impact, and behavior after remediation.

The Official Fix

Microsoft’s fix is direct: enforce the limit with ValueCount instead of KeyCount.

- if (accumulator.KeyCount > HeadersCountLimit)
+ if (accumulator.ValueCount > HeadersCountLimit)
  {
      throw new InvalidDataException(
          $"Multipart headers count limit {HeadersCountLimit} exceeded.");
  }

The related API documentation now explicitly defines the setting as a limit on header lines per multipart section and states that repeated names count separately. The patch also adds regression coverage for repeated names, case variants of the same name, zero limits, mixed names, and multiple sections. The complete change is available in the public commit: Enforce multipart header line count limits.

Affected Versions and Remediation

According to the Microsoft security advisory, the fixed versions are:

.NET / ASP.NET Core branch Affected through Fixed version
8.0 8.0.33 8.0.34
9.0 9.0.22 9.0.23
10.0 10.0.14 10.0.15
11.0 Preview / RC 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 11.0.0

The affected surface includes ASP.NET Core runtime packages and standalone references to Microsoft.AspNetCore.WebUtilities on Windows, Linux, and macOS.

When updating:

  • For framework-dependent applications, install the applicable fixed runtime and redeploy the application.
  • If the project references Microsoft.AspNetCore.WebUtilities directly, update the package, rebuild, and redeploy.
  • Self-contained applications carry their own runtime, so updating only the machine-wide runtime does not replace the embedded copy.
  • Updating only the SDK or restarting the application does not update app-local standalone package references.

Disclosure Timeline

Date Event
2026-09-01 Submitted the report and two minimal probe projects to MSRC; assigned VULN-218979 / Case 142474
2026-09-02 Added end-to-end Kestrel evidence, a concurrency ladder, and duplicate-key root-cause controls
2026-10-01 Microsoft engineering confirmed the reported behavior
2026-10-02 MSRC assessed the issue as Important / DoS and awarded a $10,000 bounty
2026-10-28 MSRC assigned CVE-2026-114149 and scheduled the fix for the November security release
2026-11-10 Microsoft published the advisory and fix, acknowledging n0irx

Lessons Learned

The final code change is one line, but the path from noticing suspicious code to receiving a bounty was mostly about building evidence.

The easiest mistake would have been to label the difference between “distinct names” and “header lines” as a vulnerability immediately. A semantic discrepancy is only an observation. It becomes a complete security finding when untrusted input can use it to defeat a control with a clear security purpose and produce a stable, attributable impact.

Another lesson is that amplification ratios need explicit denominators. Cumulative allocation, live heap, working set, and request size are different measurements and should not be substituted for one another. The report used small root-cause tests and end-to-end resource measurements for different purposes: the first explained why the bypass occurred, while the second demonstrated what happened after the bypass.

Finally, a bounty is not the end of the process. The case remained under coordinated disclosure until the security update was publicly available on November 10. Giving users access to a fix before publishing technical details is part of completing the research responsibly.

References

  • Microsoft Security Advisory: CVE-2026-114149
  • .NET Announcement: CVE-2026-114149
  • Official fix: Enforce multipart header line count limits
  • CWE-770: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling

item.title: Building an AI-Assisted Penetration Testing Workspace: Why I Created It
item.description:
The Problem with Chaotic Pen Testing

Over the years, I’ve worked on dozens of penetration testing engagements, and one pattern kept bothering me: every time I started a new target, I was reinventing the wheel.

The typical workflow looked something like this:

  • Run a few tools, dump the output into a folder
  • Scribble notes in random text files
  • Find a vulnerability, write a quick PoC, forget where I saved it
  • Start the next target, do it all over again

The knowledge I gained from one engagement rarely carried over to the next. Attack patterns I’d figured out on a Spring Boot app were lost when I moved to a Laravel target. PoCs I’d crafted sat forgotten in some archive folder. Every recon started from scratch.
item.content:
The Problem with Chaotic Pen Testing

Over the years, I’ve worked on dozens of penetration testing engagements, and one pattern kept bothering me: every time I started a new target, I was reinventing the wheel.

The typical workflow looked something like this:

  • Run a few tools, dump the output into a folder
  • Scribble notes in random text files
  • Find a vulnerability, write a quick PoC, forget where I saved it
  • Start the next target, do it all over again

The knowledge I gained from one engagement rarely carried over to the next. Attack patterns I’d figured out on a Spring Boot app were lost when I moved to a Laravel target. PoCs I’d crafted sat forgotten in some archive folder. Every recon started from scratch.

I knew there had to be a better way.

What I Wanted to Fix

Three specific pain points drove me to build this workspace.

1. Knowledge Doesn’t Accumulate

Security testing generates a lot of context — what worked, what didn’t, which endpoints were interesting, which techniques bypassed the WAF. But in a traditional setup, most of this context evaporates after the engagement ends.

I wanted a system where findings from one target could inform the next. If I confirmed an IDOR pattern on a Node.js API, that pattern should be referenceable when I see a similar API six months later. The workspace needed a persistent knowledge base where attack patterns, tech-stack notes, and verified PoCs could accumulate over time.

2. The Process Was Too Ad-Hoc

Pen testing requires systematic coverage, but without a structured workflow, it’s easy to miss things. You jump between tasks — a bit of recon here, a quick test there — and before you know it, you’ve tested the interesting stuff but skipped the boring-but-critical checks.

I wanted a workflow that enforced structure without being rigid. A clear path from recon to exploitation to evidence collection, with checkpoints along the way. Something that said “you’ve done recon, now here’s what to do with it” rather than leaving me staring at a terminal wondering what’s next.

3. Tool Sprawl Kills Productivity

Every security researcher has a tools directory that looks like a flea market. tools/ filled with random scripts, half-baked exploits, and PoCs from five years ago that may or may not still work. Finding the right tool for the job takes as long as doing the job itself.

I wanted to move from a tool-centric workflow to a skill-centric one. Instead of asking “which tool do I use for SSRF?”, ask “what’s my SSRF methodology?” and let the workspace load the right techniques, payloads, and references automatically.

How the Workspace Addresses These Problems

The workspace isn’t revolutionary — it’s just organized around a few key principles that fix the common failure points I kept hitting.

Structured Target Lifecycle

Every engagement gets a dedicated directory under targets/ with a standardized layout — scope, recon, findings, exploits, notes, report. Nothing gets lost because there’s a designated home for everything. The workflow files (workflows/new_target.md, workflows/parallel_recon.md, etc.) guide you through each phase without dictating exactly what to do.

The Skill Library Replaces Tool Scatters

Instead of hunting for the right script, I mapped vulnerability classes to hunt skills in HUNT_INDEX.md. When recon surfaces a technology stack, I load the matching skill — and it brings the methodology, payloads, and references for that vulnerability class. It’s not magic, it’s just organized.

For example, when I see a GraphQL endpoint, I load hunt-graphql. It has GraphQL-specific introspection queries, batching attack patterns, and known mitigation bypasses. No more Googling “how to test GraphQL” every single time.

The Knowledge Base Grows Over Time

The kb/ directory is designed to accumulate. Technical stack notes go in kb/stacks/. Verified vulnerability patterns go in kb/patterns/. Completed target writeups go in kb/targets/. Each engagement adds to the collective knowledge rather than starting from zero.

A simple heuristic drives this: if a vulnerability was confirmed on two targets of the same stack, it’s likely present on the third until proven otherwise. The knowledge base makes that heuristic actionable.

What It’s Not

This workspace isn’t a replacement for skill or experience. It doesn’t automate finding vulnerabilities. What it does is reduce the overhead around the actual work — the organizing, the remembering, the context-switching — so you can focus on what matters: understanding the target and finding the flaws.

It’s also not a “beginner’s toolkit.” It assumes you know how to test; it just helps you do it more systematically.

The Result

After using this workspace for a while, the difference is noticeable. Starting a new target isn’t a blank slate anymore — it’s “I’ve seen this stack before, let me check what I learned last time.” Findings don’t disappear after the engagement ends; they become reference material for the next one. The process has structure without being suffocating.

That’s really the whole point. Less overhead, more accumulated knowledge, fewer things falling through the cracks.
